title: ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN URBAN SOUNDSCAPE PERCEPTION AND EMOTIONAL STATES
authors: Maria Luiza de Ulhôa Carvalho et al., 2023
research_question: The aim of this thesis is to investigate the relationships between soundscape perception and emotional state in urban locations (park, plaza, and pedestrian street) that may indicate changes on responses to the sonic environment. Specifically: 1. How can real-time EEG measurements be compatible with VR method in urban soundscape studies? 2. How to overcome electric line noise in EEG data originated from VR HMD? 3. How does different human occupancy and nature sound in different urban scenarios effect EEG alpha power? 4. Can higher educated individuals differ in brain activity when assessing urban soundscapes through VR? 5. Can the university community identify places that represent the ISO’s 4 PAQs quadrants? 6. Can the number of people shift ISO’s PAQ responses in different urban areas? 7. Can children’s sounds induce vibrancy?

participants.description: 36 participants (64% men and 36% women, average age 32±10) from 11 different countries (47% UK, 17% India, 6% each from Brazil, Chile, China, Poland, 3% each from Ecuador, Egypt, Iran, Myanmar, Pakistan). 75% spoke 1-2 languages, 25% 3+ languages. 86% had level 6+ education. 64% had acoustic/musical background. 97% reported no hearing loss, 83% no tinnitus.
participants.recruitment: Individuals on the mailing list of the Acoustic Research Centre of Salford (ARC) with connections to the University of Salford, above 18 years old, recruited over the internet on social networks. Compensated with £25 Amazon voucher for 2h30 experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Mental imagery of public spaces in Manchester based on recall for Experiment 1.
Peel Park and Clifford Whitworth Library in situ for Experiment 2.
30-second audio-visual samples of Piccadilly Gardens at empty, medium, and busy population densities for Experiment 3 (pilot).

1-minute 360° videos with spatial audio of Piccadilly Gardens (Plaza), Market Street (Street), a bus stop, and Peel Park (Park) at empty, medium, and busy population densities for Experiment 4 (online).

8-second audio-visual samples of Piccadilly Gardens (Plaza), Market Street (Street), and Peel Park (Park) at empty and busy population densities, 32 repeats per condition, for Experiment 5 (EEG-VR lab).

measures.instrument: PANAS (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule) with 10 emotional states
ISO’s PAQs (Pleasant to Unpleasant, Eventful to Uneventful, Vibrant to Monotonous, Calm to Chaotic) on an 11-point Likert scale (Exp 3) or slider from -10 to +10 (Exp 4) or 0 to 100 (Exp 5).
Self-Assessment Manikins (SAM) for Valence, Arousal, and Dominance on a 5-point Likert scale
Plutchik’s wheel of emotions (32 emotional options)
Electroencephalogram (EEG) Alpha Power (µV²/Hz) from 32 electrodes across 10 brain regions

findings.antecedent: Public places in Manchester
findings.consequent: Identification of soundscape types (Vibrant, Calm, Monotonous, Chaotic)
findings.quote: The final selections are marked by the orange rectangle. They were Piccadilly Gardens (popular city centre plaza) for the Vibrant, Peel Park (park in the University of Salford) for the Calm, a bus stop (common bus stop in front of the University of Salford) for the Monotonous, and Market Street (pedestrian shopping street) for the Chaotic soundscape.

findings.antecedent: Piccadilly Gardens
findings.mechanism: The appearance of the same location in more than one PAQ category indicated other factors within the same site are influencing soundscape perception.
findings.quote: Piccadilly Gardens appeared in the Chaotic, Vibrant, and Calm quadrants with respectively six, four, and one vote.

findings.antecedent: Train Station
findings.mechanism: When considered Chaotic, the location was related to traffic noise as screeching of trains and horns in participants answers. For the Monotonous scale, unfortunately, some participants left answers blank with no explanation.
findings.quote: The Train Station appeared the same number of times for Chaotic and Monotonous PAQs.

findings.antecedent: Location (Peel Park vs. Clifford Whitworth Library)
findings.mechanism: the park was considered more calming than the library, possibly because of its benefits for stress recovery due to natural sounds (Payne, 2013).
findings.quote: A total of 11 parameters from the 19 descriptors were significantly different at a p-value of 0.05 or lower. These descriptors with significant differences had a superior mean rank for the park except for the directional-universal soundscape descriptors.

findings.antecedent: Location (Peel Park vs. Clifford Whitworth Library)
findings.mechanism: People in the library presented to be more “upset” in the place, possibly related to the academic environment where tension is present while studying for assessment and exams. Also, they may feel more “determined” to develop intellectual tasks in the library than a public place. People also felt more “inspired” and “active” in the park.
findings.quote: From the 10 states, only upset, inspired, determined, and active had a significant difference among the park and library.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Piccadilly Gardens
findings.mechanism: population density increase effected positively the eventful and vibrant scales. eventful soundscapes as full of human activity.
findings.quote: As the population density increased so did the ratings from uneventful-eventful and monotonous-vibrant scales.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Piccadilly Gardens
findings.mechanism: population density increase effected positively the eventful and vibrant scales
findings.quote: As the population density increased so did the ratings from uneventful-eventful and monotonous-vibrant scales.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Piccadilly Gardens
findings.mechanism: when the number of people incremented in the plaza scores decreased in the chaotic to calm PAQ with a significant negative effect between empty-busy and medium-busy.
findings.quote: population density increase effected positively the eventful and vibrant scales, while negatively the calm scores

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Piccadilly Gardens
findings.mechanism: an experimental error was identified in the medium density sample, where the audio was not calibrated and louder than the empty and busy scenarios. Therefore, the significance in the pleasant scale of the medium population density result was associated with the disproportional sound level of the sample.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Piccadilly Gardens
findings.quote: Only the “active” emotional state had a significant difference among conditions with a positive effect among the empty-busy and medium-busy conditions. That is, people rated more towards always “active” when population density increased

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Park
findings.mechanism: urban parks represent an ecosystem with predominant natural elements... these locations need a reduced presence of people to preserve natural urban areas for the local fauna and flora, and to provide possible places for human restoration (Payne, 2013).
findings.quote: At the Park, the increased number of people significantly diminishes the perception of calmness towards a perception of chaos (Figure 47a).

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Park
findings.mechanism: a sense of calmness appeared in the absence of people for the empty and medium conditions at the Park
findings.quote: Also present in the aroused emotional state, a sense of calmness appeared in the absence of people for the empty and medium conditions at the Park (Figure 47b).

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Plaza
findings.mechanism: The increase in the eventful ratings with the number of people at the Plaza (Figure 48a) and the Street (Figure 49a) corroborates with the description of the Eventful places in part 3 of the soundscape ISO 12913-3 (PD ISO 12913-3, 2019).
findings.quote: as population density increased, so did the eventful responses at the Plaza and Street, corroborating the ISO 12913-3 (PD ISO 12913-3, 2019) description of eventful places.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Plaza
findings.mechanism: the shift in the perceived soundscape quality from monotony to vibrancy at the Plaza (Figure 48b) when more individuals are in the scene, confirms the initial site selection representing a vibrant scenario in Manchester (Session 4.1).
findings.quote: the Monotonous to Vibrant PAQ at the Plaza, but decreased the ratings on the Chaotic to Calm PAQs at the Park.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Street
findings.mechanism: The increase in the eventful ratings with the number of people at the Plaza (Figure 48a) and the Street (Figure 49a) corroborates with the description of the Eventful places in part 3 of the soundscape ISO 12913-3 (PD ISO 12913-3, 2019).
findings.quote: as population density increased, so did the eventful responses at the Plaza and Street, corroborating the ISO 12913-3 (PD ISO 12913-3, 2019) description of eventful places.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Street
findings.mechanism: a change in this emotional state was significant with the increase of people on the Street. However, the medians varied from a more neutral score in the empty condition to an excited and alert state in the busy condition (Figure 49b)
findings.quote: Likewise, a change in this emotional state was significant with the increase of people on the Street.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Bus Stop
findings.mechanism: The bus stop outcome was monotonous independently of the number of individuals in the scene, corroborating the previous selection of the site as a monotonous place (Session 4.1).
findings.quote: All semantic parameters changed with the different number of people in all locations except for the Monotonous to Vibrant PAQs at the bus stop and the dominance scale at the Street.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty, medium, busy) in Street
findings.mechanism: the dominance scale consistency independently of the number of individuals at Market Street still needs further investigation if the indifference of the rating demonstrated a lack of understanding of the term or the absence of a sense of safety due to the proximity to people walking by the street
findings.quote: All semantic parameters changed with the different number of people in all locations except for the Monotonous to Vibrant PAQs at the bus stop and the dominance scale at the Street.

findings.antecedent: Nationality (Brazilian vs. Non-Brazilian)
findings.mechanism: may be related to cultural differences, unknown European scenarios, and non-validated translations of PAQ words into Portuguese.
findings.quote: Brazilians demonstrated to rate significantly higher the listed semantic scales except on the Monotonous to Vibrant PAQ for the medium and busy conditions at the Street, and the same PAQ for the medium condition at the bus stop.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty vs. busy) in Plaza
findings.consequent: PAQ ratings (Annoying, Chaotic, Eventful, Vibrant, Calm, Pleasant, Uneventful, Monotonous)
findings.mechanism: PAQ ratings increased when locations were busy for the Annoying PAQ at the Plaza and Street, the Chaotic PAQ at the Plaza, the Vibrant PAQ at the Plaza and Park, the Monotonous and Uneventful PAQs at the Street and Park, and the Eventful PAQ at all locations. Meanwhile, Calm and Pleasant scores decreased with the number of people in all locations.
findings.quote: All PAQs significantly changed with population density.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty vs. busy) in Park
findings.consequent: PAQ ratings (Chaotic, Eventful, Vibrant, Calm, Pleasant, Uneventful, Monotonous)
findings.mechanism: PAQ ratings increased when locations were busy for the Annoying PAQ at the Plaza and Street, the Chaotic PAQ at the Plaza, the Vibrant PAQ at the Plaza and Park, the Monotonous and Uneventful PAQs at the Street and Park, and the Eventful PAQ at all locations. Meanwhile, Calm and Pleasant scores decreased with the number of people in all locations.
findings.quote: All PAQ results changed with population density except for the Annoying PAQ at the Park and the Vibrant PAQ at the Street.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty vs. busy) in Street
findings.consequent: PAQ ratings (Annoying, Chaotic, Eventful, Calm, Pleasant, Uneventful, Monotonous)
findings.mechanism: PAQ ratings increased when locations were busy for the Annoying PAQ at the Plaza and Street, the Chaotic PAQ at the Plaza, the Vibrant PAQ at the Plaza and Park, the Monotonous and Uneventful PAQs at the Street and Park, and the Eventful PAQ at all locations. Meanwhile, Calm and Pleasant scores decreased with the number of people in all locations.
findings.quote: All PAQ results changed with population density except for the Annoying PAQ at the Park and the Vibrant PAQ at the Street.

findings.antecedent: Location (Park vs. Plaza vs. Street) in same population density
findings.mechanism: dissimilarities in PAQ ratings among locations would be expected given they are different sites with distinct urban functions and context. Therefore, observing similar PAQ results becomes relevant in terms of non-significant results.
findings.quote: the comparison of PAQ results among locations demonstrated that the Park and Street were the most distinct locations while the Park and Plaza shared more similarities.

findings.antecedent: Busy Plaza (with children playing on water fountain)
findings.mechanism: The concept of these emotions may carry resemblances with the PAQs where joyfulness relates to vibrancy and serenity to calmness. high pitch sounds from their screams and sounds of water
findings.quote: Only the busy Plaza and empty Park had statistically significant proportion in the selected emotions with over half participants perceiving the scenario with "joy" (19 individuals, ꭓ2(3) = 15.778, p = 0.001)

findings.antecedent: Empty Park (with bird calls)
findings.mechanism: The concept of these emotions may carry resemblances with the PAQs where joyfulness relates to vibrancy and serenity to calmness. empty spaces evoked “serenity” in Plutchik’s emotion wheel which can be associated with states of calmness. Note that these locations also had predominant sounds of nature.
findings.quote: and “serenity” (23 participants, ꭓ2(3) = 30.00, p < 0.001) respectively.

findings.antecedent: Empty locations (Park and Plaza)
findings.consequent: EEG Alpha Power at occipital regions
findings.mechanism: alpha brain waves can be induced at the posterior brain regions by relaxation and drowsiness (Teplan, 2002), the increased values of alpha power at occipital regions in empty locations may indicate participants were more relaxed when there were no people in the scene.
findings.quote: a similar increasing tendency when locations were empty was observed in alpha power. This observation led to further investigation towards alpha power.

findings.antecedent: Population density (empty vs. busy)
findings.consequent: EEG Alpha Power at middle parietal, middle occipital, and right occipital regions (for both clusters)
findings.mechanism: middle parietal, middle and right occipital regions demonstrated significant effect of population density in alpha power results for both clustered groups. increased values of alpha power at occipital regions in empty locations may indicate participants were more relaxed when there were no people in the scene.
findings.quote: middle parietal, middle and right occipital regions demonstrated significant effect of population density in alpha power results for both clustered groups.

findings.antecedent: Educational level (higher education)
findings.consequent: EEG Alpha Power responses to population density conditions (8 out of 10 brain regions)
findings.mechanism: This result may indicate an effect of educational level on EEG responses of participants with higher education demonstrating more consensus in brain activity than those with lower education level.
findings.quote: participants from EEG cluster 2 were predominantly highly educated individuals, and eight out of 10 brain regions had significant differences in population density conditions, whilst cluster 1 had only three regions significantly different.

findings.antecedent: Empty Park with bird calls
findings.mechanism: This behaviour was also observed in Li, Ba and Kang’s study where increased values of α-EEG reactivity was observed for sea and bird sounds when compared to street and traffic sounds (Li and Kang, 2019). empty Peel Park may represent a location for relaxation given reports of evoked emotions of serenity and high values of alpha power at occipital regions.
findings.quote: From another perspective, the empty Park with bird calls as predominant sound sources had high values of EEG alpha power.

findings.antecedent: Piccadilly Gardens (water fountain)
findings.mechanism: current EEG alpha power findings at Peel Park (bird calls) and Piccadilly Gardens (water fountain) go in line with other works, such as Li et al. for water (Li et al., 2022), and Li, Xie, and Woodward for bird call sounds (Li, Xie and Woodward, 2021), but are not identical to cited studies.
findings.quote: current EEG alpha power findings at Peel Park (bird calls) and Piccadilly Gardens (water fountain) go in line with other works

findings.antecedent: Visual cues from VR HMD
findings.consequent: EEG Alpha Power in occipital regions
findings.mechanism: visual cues are also processed in this area, indicating that the results of higher alpha power values in the occipital regions require caution as a statement due to the possibility that the activation comes from the visual stimuli from the VR HMD and not necessarily from the soundscape audio-visual stimuli.
findings.quote: visual cues are also processed in this area, indicating that the results of higher alpha power values in the occipital regions require caution as a statement due to the possibility that the activation comes from the visual stimuli from the VR HMD

mechanisms: population density changes perceptual and emotional responses in urban soundscapes
alpha brain waves can be induced at the posterior brain regions by relaxation and drowsiness
increased values of alpha power at occipital regions in empty locations may indicate participants were more relaxed when there were no people in the scene
The concept of these emotions [joy, serenity] may carry resemblances with the PAQs where joyfulness relates to vibrancy and serenity to calmness
educational level on EEG responses of participants with higher education demonstrating more consensus in brain activity
implementation_implications: population density and the design of Plazas should be considered in assessing, planning, and designing urban soundscapes towards livelier sounding cities.
The benefits from this kind of research impact not only alternative solutions for environmental noise issues, but also improvements in public health, quality of life, and cultural heritage.
busy Plazas should also be integrated to the options of urban soundscape interventions along with empty parks.
Plazas should be considered as a soundscape design tool, just as parks already are.
support urban planning and design in enhancing existing or new urban areas into better-sounding cities using green areas and water features to bring birds and create pleasant sounds of water.

limitations: Experiment 1: The Train Station required formal authorization for recordings which was not granted, leading to its abandonment as a study location.

Experiment 2: Some participants demonstrated impatience to respond to the 20 soundscape descriptors. Fewer participants in the park than the library. Some individuals avoided answering the survey due to the number of elements to read.

Experiment 3 (pilot): Uncontrolled experimental environment, small sample size, noises interfering with the experiment, and uncalibrated samples. An experimental error was identified in the medium density sample, where the audio was not calibrated and was louder than the empty and busy scenarios.

Experiment 4 (online): Difficulties with face-to-face experiments during the pandemic led to an online approach. Video resolutions were considered poor, leading to new recordings for the EEG VR test. Lack of controlled laboratory conditions (e.g., constant audio/video reproduction system), efficient acoustic laboratory settings, and consistent contact between researcher and participant.

Experiment 5 (EEG-VR lab): Experimental duration with 40 stimuli repeats became exhausting for participants, leading to reduction to 32 repeats. Gamma band had small absolute power for both individuals, leading to its elimination from analysis. Expressive difference in Absolute Power among participants. Cluster analysis demonstrated different groupings for each of the six stimuli, preventing further investigations to compare group differences per condition. Visual cues are also processed in the occipital region, so higher alpha power values in this area require caution as activation might come from visual stimuli from the VR HMD, not necessarily from soundscape audio-visual stimuli. Differences in experimental design compared to related work (Jeon, Jo and Lee, 2023) regarding participant mental state control, urban scenarios, stimuli duration, and physiological metrics (e.g., EEG ratio vs. alpha power).
